text: [sighs] Regarding the subject of avoiding foods and eating, and since Dr. Diaa Al-Awady—may God have mercy on him—
My experience is different from anyone else following the system, and you will understand why when I tell you.
He himself knew that, may God have mercy on him. He used to tell me, 'For me, you are different from anyone else following my system.'
I am a chemist, class of 2003. I studied chemistry and biology, and my work was in medical laboratory analysis and parasitology.
I also worked in chemistry testing. Anyway, in 2016 I got an infection from the laboratory.
The left side of my face became extremely swollen, so I went to be examined.
The pain was terrible. The doctor asked for an MRI, and when I gave him the result he said we needed to do
surgery immediately because I had what he described as a bacterial mass at the base of the skull that could rupture at any moment, and that if it ruptured I could die within
seconds because it was in a dangerous area close to the brain, and if the bacteria reached the brain they might not be able to save me.
He said they would remove it, but it could come back once or twice a year, possibly three times, because I smoked, so I needed to quit smoking to reduce the recurrence.
Instead of three times, maybe once or twice. I took my reports from him and left.
This doctor had followed me since childhood and treated me for sinus allergies, and there was another doctor
who treated me for chest allergies because I had seasonal allergies. With changes of season, my breathing would become difficult and I needed treatment.
Anyway, I went to another consultant and showed him the reports. He said the same thing. That same day I saw four consultants: my regular doctor
whom I had known since I was a child, plus three others. All of them said I needed surgery immediately and that afterward I would have to wear a face shield
and avoid perfumes, cigarettes, and practically everything around me.
They told me not to be exposed to pollution. I thought, how can anyone avoid pollution when we are surrounded by it?
I went to a friend of mine who was the fifth doctor I consulted. I told her I wanted a solution and that I did not want surgery. She said,
'Let's try medication for a month.' I agreed. She wrote a prescription and I looked at it.
By the way, before I worked in the laboratory I had worked for a pharmaceutical company, so I had actually
worked with medicines in the lab. If you tell me the active ingredient, I can usually tell you what the medicine does.
Do not just tell me the brand name; tell me the active ingredient, because that was part of my work.
Anyway, she prescribed cortisone. The doctor who had treated me since childhood had also treated me
with cortisone for chest allergies, but it had been a treatment course that was tapered gradually. I had taken
cortisone before without problems, so from a young age I knew that it usually should be tapered rather than stopped suddenly.
She prescribed cortisone for a month. I asked, 'How will we stop it afterward?' She said we would simply stop it.
I thought, 'You do not understand this either.' I took the prescription as I was leaving,
tore it up, did not fill it, went home, and prayed: 'God, I belong to You. If I am going to die, then I am going to die.'
'If this is my appointed time, I accept it. But if You have written that I will recover and still have life ahead of me, then, God,
I will not ask another person. You show me how to recover.' I surrendered the matter to God.
Two things came to my mind: the saying 'Fast and you will be healthy,' and the Qur'anic phrase about fruit and bird meat that people desire.
Those were the two things.
I opened the Qur'an and found the verse, and I understood it as food described for the people of Paradise.
I said, 'All right, God: fasting and fruit. But what exactly is bird meat?' I started analyzing it because I am a chemist and a science person.
In biology we studied the animal kingdom and how classifications are made.
We learned that a bird is an animal that flies through the air by beating its wings, while poultry such as ducks and chickens
and turkeys have feathers and wings but do not necessarily fly in the same way, yet they are classified
with birds because they have similar external and anatomical characteristics.
So I started asking myself what the word 'bird' really meant in this context.
I looked up the Arabic word and found definitions referring to what rises into the air by beating its wings.
So I thought of things like pigeons and quail, but I did not have the energy to go searching for those foods.
I decided to focus on fruit. It was winter, around February.
There was not much fruit available—mainly apples, bananas, oranges, and mandarins.
For a full month I practiced intermittent fasting and drank green coffee and Arabic coffee. I would put two slices of ginger in the mug,
and make the coffee with cinnamon, cloves, and turmeric. I would drink it and it reduced my appetite.
I would eat one or two apples, and that was almost all I ate during the day. During that month, the swelling in my face—which had been severe enough to close one eye—started to
calm down and decrease. I wanted to understand what was happening because I could feel some improvement but did not know why.
You can imagine how frightened I was, because the last doctor had told me we would try treatment
for a month, but that I should stay home, avoid vigorous movement, and even avoid tossing around in my sleep so my head would not move too much.
She said I should not bump my head because the mass might rupture at any moment. Imagine spending a whole month at home
thinking you might die at any moment.
Anyway, I went back to her. She asked for another MRI. She could see that the swelling and pain had decreased and that the mass seemed smaller.
But it was still there. It had been large enough, according to what I was told, to affect the density of the facial bones.
It had affected the bone density around my skull. I had another MRI and brought her the report. She said, 'Thank God, the treatment worked.'
I had not told her what I was actually doing. I only said I felt better and asked what we should do next. She said to repeat the MRI.
She assumed I was taking the prescribed treatment, so she suggested another month. Inside, I was thanking God.
After another month the mass was smaller again. I continued for another month and had another MRI.
It kept getting smaller. After three more months, making four months in total, the final
MRI showed that the mass had disappeared. Thank God, it has not returned up to now. And here is the surprising part: I had not yet
quit smoking. I only stopped smoking before Ramadan some time after that. In 2016, while I was fasting and eating fruit,
I was still smoking two packs a day of Captain Black little cigars—the black ones. Anyone who smokes knows
those are very strong cigarettes. I was smoking two packs a day even though the doctors had told me I needed to stop smoking and avoid everything
because they believed the problem would recur once or twice a year. Yet during those four months, I say that I recovered from it, and it did not return, even while I was still smoking.
I had another health problem even before the mass, and I had been living with it.
In 2008 I developed a problem in my lumbar vertebrae that caused temporary paralysis in my legs; suddenly my legs would become paralyzed.
Four of the lower vertebrae were involved, and the two middle ones were very close together and pressing near
the motor nerve. This is how the orthopedic doctor explained it to me. When I exerted myself or moved the wrong way,
the pressure would increase on the motor nerve and cause paralysis in both legs. He said I needed surgery. That was in 2008, and I refused
the operation. I respect medicine and doctors, but I have always had this particular conviction—I know I can be stubborn.
When I was young I used to ask my mother, 'Why do I go to a doctor if the doctor himself gets sick? He studied medicine, so why
does he become ill? If he studied medicine, shouldn't he know how not to get sick? We get sick because we are not doctors—so why does he?'
I used to tell my mother that if doctors themselves become ill, then perhaps they do not have everything that can help me. That was my way of thinking.
I have always preferred to use my own mind and take responsibility for my choices and their consequences.
So I followed my own judgment rather than simply following someone else's, and I felt that God opened a path for me.
Then I noticed that my back no longer hurt.
The day I learned the mass had disappeared and I believed I had recovered, I was so happy
that I started jumping around. Before that, I had been told not to bend down or lift
anything heavy, and even stepping off a treadmill had to be done carefully.
But that day I was jumping onto the sofa, off the sofa, onto chairs and beds—literally jumping around the house from happiness.
All I could say was, 'Thank God, thank God.' I was crying and jumping.
Then suddenly I remembered that I supposedly had a serious back problem. I froze and thought, 'God protect me—my back is going to hurt again now.'
I stayed completely still for maybe half an hour, waiting for something to happen, but there was no pain.
There was no discomfort. I had also had sciatica, and anyone with sciatica knows what exertion can do.
Yet I had spent half an hour jumping around from happiness and crying with joy.
Nothing happened. I went to be examined and was told there was no new problem.
The vertebral abnormality was still present, but I was told the nerve itself was not damaged by the closeness of the vertebrae.
The nerve was no longer being affected in the same way, even though previously the pressure had caused severe symptoms.
That pressure had once caused paralysis. I also had wear in my neck and used to wear a neck brace.
I wore it for perhaps a year or two. I could not turn my neck quickly in either direction. My spine
felt damaged at the top and bottom, while the middle section was the only part that seemed relatively normal.
Can you imagine how I was living and how carefully I had to move because of my back?
Before I felt better overall, the bacterial mass had happened, and during that same period I felt that
all those bone pains and problems improved as well.
My interpretation was that when I removed what I believed was harming me, my body was finally able to heal itself—even while I was smoking.
Even though I was still smoking. After those four months I thought, 'That's it.'
When I later told Dr. Diaa this story, may God have mercy on him, he said to me something like, 'You went down into a one-on-one fight with death.'
'It was you or it—one of you had to defeat the other.' When you come out of something like that, you see life differently.
I felt as though my back was against the wall and death was in front of me: either me or it.
And by God's mercy, I believed I had overcome it.
More accurately, I believed God had removed it. I felt well, I could jump and exercise, and I returned to working out. I was not someone who liked gyms; I preferred doing
everything at home. I had my own equipment and would put on headphones and exercise for two to two and a half hours, even with weights on my legs.
My back did not hurt. My shoulders, neck, and back felt fine. I also noticed
that I no longer had body odor from sweating, and at first I did not understand why. Later, after hearing Dr. Diaa
explain his ideas, I understood it according to his interpretation: that when the body is 'clean,' a person can sweat without
a strong odor, and that he attributed unpleasant sweat odor to diet.
During those four months, I also noticed that after washing for prayer in the morning, I sometimes went most of
the day without needing to wash again unless I used the bathroom. I would wash only once or twice a day and noticed very little odor.
I thought, 'God created us clean.' I used to ask, 'God, You made everything beautifully—why would You create us with such unpleasant smells?'
I used to wonder why people have foul-smelling gas and other unpleasant bodily odors.
Then I came to believe there should not normally be strong-smelling gas, and that if gas occurs it should have little or no odor.
I took this as a sign, in my own interpretation, of digestive health.
I noticed something else: throughout my life I had problems with my hormones.
My periods had never been regular, but suddenly they became so regular that I could almost set a clock by them.
I had always asked God about this and had struggled with the idea: 'Why are women created to suffer like this?'
I would say, 'Help me understand. I am not rejecting it; I just want to understand why women would suffer for
an entire month—two weeks feeling normal and another two weeks emotionally overwhelmed,
making decisions that could damage their lives or upset husbands, children, family, siblings,
or work. Surely there must be something wrong; surely women were not created to suffer like this just to have children.'
Then, during those four months, I personally stopped experiencing what I considered PMS symptoms such as cramps, back pain, bloating,
depression, anxiety, or similar symptoms. Then I started thinking about expanding what I ate.
During those four months I kept reading and researching. One of the topics I looked into was vitamin D, and I came across
In the U.S., I found what I understood to be a functional-medicine organization.
As I understood it, people there could choose conventional or functional medicine, each at their own responsibility.
I read about raising vitamin D levels to around 100–125, and because I worked in lab testing I was used to reading reference ranges.
The reference range I knew said roughly 30–70 was good, while levels above 100 were labeled toxic.
So I wondered what 70–100 meant—if I reached 100, would that be toxic or normal?
Later I saw the toxicity threshold described as above 150.
Then I wondered what 100–150 meant and why that range was not being discussed.
I had my vitamin D tested and it came back at 13, during those four months.
I decided to raise my vitamin D substantially. I am not telling anyone else to do this; I was making my own decision as a chemist.
I felt God was guiding me, and I had developed a sense of how to deal with my body.
I listened closely to my body and tried to understand what it was telling me.
I took what I considered very high doses of vitamin D and raised my level to around 70 during those four months.
I continued the same dose for a while and honestly stopped checking the level regularly; this was alongside fasting and fruit.
I felt my chest allergy and sinus symptoms disappeared. Then I wanted to expand what I ate.
I kept researching, and during those four months I also lost about 30 kilograms.
I am 152 cm tall and had always carried much more weight in my lower body than my upper body.
Before losing weight I was in the 70-kilogram range, and whenever I lost weight it never seemed proportional.
My lower body stayed much larger than my upper body; I used to joke that if I weighed 75 kilos, five were on top and seventy below.
I eventually went down to—
about 54 kilograms, so depending on the starting point that was roughly 20 to 30 kilograms lost.
For the first time in my life, I felt my body was proportionate.
I had time to read, research, and contact doctors and universities abroad to understand what others were doing.
One idea I came across was that my body-fat distribution might be related to
high estrogen, and I formed the belief that synthetic estrogens entering the body could interfere with normal hormone metabolism.
In my interpretation, estrogen could then accumulate and affect body-fat distribution.
I asked where synthetic estrogen exposure might come from and became concerned about milk and dairy products from what I had read.
So I said, 'Fine, I will stop drinking milk and eating dairy products.'
Then I read more about casein, a storage protein in milk, and found many claims about possible effects; I have posted some of that material.
Anyway, without making this too long, I followed my own dietary approach from 2016 until
2022, and during that period I felt excellent.
I felt healthy and energetic until friends around me started encouraging me to eat
various foods again, saying my restrictions were unhealthy. I began adding foods back.
After those first four months I added fried potatoes because I love them, and I felt fine after eating them.
I did not notice immediate negative effects, and by then I had started paying close attention to how food
affected my body. Because I often ate one main meal, I felt I could identify which food caused a reaction.
The potatoes seemed fine, and fruit was already fine, so I continued them. Then I ate
chicken—breaded fried chicken, which I love—and afterward I noticed
that my mood suddenly felt worse and irritable, and my back
started to ache slightly. At first I did not connect it to the food.
A couple of days later I had mild abdominal cramps, so I searched for information about chicken because it was the main new food.
I read claims that chickens can be exposed to synthetic hormones during production.
I thought I had put synthetic hormones into my body and blamed that for how I felt.
I decided I did not like how I felt and stopped eating chicken again.
These were my own personal experiments; I did not know Dr. Diaa yet. This was around 2016–2018.
During those months I built my own ideas. People would ask, 'So what were you eating?'
Potatoes and eggs were among the foods I relied on. Eggs sometimes bothered me too, but I felt I had few alternatives.
I had heard many warnings that rice was dangerous or unhealthy, so at the time I mostly avoided it.
I mainly ate potatoes and only occasionally ate rice.
I ate eggs, and fruit was a major part of my diet; I might make a fruit salad with ice cream and enjoy that as a meal.
Later friends convinced me to have a street-style fava-bean-and-egg sandwich.
I love street fava beans and they knew it, so I ate the sandwich.
It had bread, beans, and eggs—a combination I loved. After years without bread, tasting it again was overwhelming.
It felt like a relapse after a long period of abstaining, and I started eating more.
What I am about to describe happened over about six months. For the first three months
I had no obvious symptoms and ate a fava-bean-and-egg sandwich almost every day.
I also kept eating fruit and potatoes. After about three months my stomach began to bother me and my back pain returned.
The old back pain, sciatica, and sinus symptoms came back. This was around
2022, and people around me told me I was not eating properly and probably lacked vitamins.
They kept telling me to eat vegetables and drink green juice, so I tried it.
I drank the green juice and felt terrible afterward; I described the reaction as so severe that I felt as if I were dying.
Then I tried other foods people considered light or healthy, including cottage cheese, but I felt very unwell after eating it.
While I was eating cottage cheese and scrolling through Facebook, I saw someone speaking very passionately in a video.
I recognized that kind of passion because when someone truly believes they are defending what is right, it shows.
I asked myself, 'Who is this person who is so worked up about this?' It turned out to be Al-Awady.
I thought he was making sense, so I went to see him and took along a colleague with rheumatoid arthritis whom I had spent years trying to persuade
to stop bread and dairy because I believed those foods were harming him. He had reduced them somewhat but had not
stopped his medications. I took him with me to Dr. Diaa and told him, 'You are right. I know you are right,' then explained my experience.
I told him my full story. I also understood what he meant when he made provocative statements about smoking.
He was not literally saying smoking had no harm; my understanding was that he meant the body can sometimes
recover despite the harmful effects of smoking if other things he considered more harmful were removed from the diet.
I used my own experience as an example: I had been told I had a bacterial mass at the base of the skull.
I had also had sinus problems, which doctors had linked to laboratory exposure and smoking.
Yet I believed I recovered while still smoking, so I concluded—rightly or wrongly—that smoking had not been the main cause in my case.
I was also eating fried potatoes cooked in hydrogenated oils. When you went to his clinic, he did not actually prescribe hydrogenated oils.
Anyone following his plan knew he did not write that on the diet sheet; my point is that people misunderstood what he meant.
People would take half a statement and remove it from context.
Someone might open a live video, hear two sentences, and immediately say, 'This man does not understand anything,' because they heard someone else say so.
Then everyone repeats the same judgment without hearing the full explanation or dealing with him personally.
I traveled from Alexandria to Cairo to sit with him, understand how he thought, and hear him explain his ideas directly.
I felt people often judged him only from the outside. He has passed away, but his ideas and system remain, and
personally I am deeply convinced by the system because of my own experience.
Not simply because it was Dr. Diaa, but because I had already gone through much of my experience before I knew him.
His explanations later gave me a framework for why I believed I had improved and what I thought happened when certain foods were removed.
Regarding statements such as 'smoking is not harmful' or 'hydrogenated oils are not harmful,' my understanding is that he did not literally say they were harmless.
He described some things as less harmful, in his view, compared with the foods he most strongly advised avoiding.
He did not tell people to take a drug. His message was about changing what they were eating and trying the diet.
And he repeatedly said not to stop medications unless they returned to him or followed a medical plan.
People who saw him, including those taking cholesterol medication, knew that he did not simply stop every drug at once.
He used a particular treatment protocol when changing medications. I felt some critics had only heard fragments rather than going for a full consultation.
Dr. Diaa's system had two main guidelines, and his videos are still available.
The first guideline, as I understood it, addressed people who mocked him by saying he told everyone to eat unlimited sugar, Nutella, or chips.
His actual point, as I understood it from the videos, was that sugar and starch should be eaten according to the body's needs.
He argued that staying within one's needs would help avoid what he called inflammatory pathways.
In other words, the amount of sugar and starch should depend on the person's lifestyle and daily activity.
Someone who sits at a desk all day will not have the same carbohydrate needs as someone doing heavy physical labor.
That seems obvious to me, but I felt many people did not try to understand or discuss the system with him directly.
The second guideline was about the list of permitted foods. He sometimes jokingly said the permitted list was 'for fun,' then explained that his main staples were potatoes and rice.
He also emphasized healthy fats and a limited amount of sugar according to the person's needs.
Those were what he considered the core foods. He even said at one point that toast did not need to be eaten every day.
His live videos are still available. His basic foods, as I understood them, were rice, potatoes, and healthy fats.
He said the rest of the permitted list was more flexible, or 'for fun,' as he jokingly put it.
He explained that if he said a food was permitted but your own body consistently reacted badly to it, you should pay attention to your body.
For example, if he said dates were permitted but they made you feel unwell, he would say your body was telling you something.
Yet suddenly people labeled him 'the Nutella doctor' or 'the sugar doctor' and claimed he was making people sick.
But people who actually visited his clinic knew, in my experience, that he did not prescribe the huge amounts of sugar critics talked about.
The main foods on his written plan were potatoes, rice, and healthy fats such as olive oil or butter.
And any dietary system in the world can have some
errors or limitations. Think about the keto diet, which was once widely promoted for insulin resistance and blood pressure.
Later, after keto became extremely popular and many people followed it,
concerns emerged about problems such as ketoacidosis in certain situations and about how long strict keto should be followed.
So people began recommending shorter periods or modified low-carb approaches, and not everyone improved.
Then people focused intensely on Al-Awady's system and criticized it. But naturally any system can have
mistakes, and different bodies can respond differently. One person may improve in a week while another may take two days; responses vary.
Health conditions are different too. He had patients with diabetes who came to him while using
insulin. According to testimonials, some reduced or stopped insulin, some went from two types to one, and some
reduced the number of daily doses. Others used insulin less frequently. Those testimonial videos are available.
I believe people should actually watch the material rather than repeating accusations.
I object to attacking people's reputation or honor unfairly. Dr. Diaa has passed away and, in my words, has gone to the Most Merciful.
I leave the matter to God.
